quote: {+wie+} Wenn jener cubische Körper die Relativdiskriminante 1 besitzt?
english: How, if that cubic field has relative discriminant 1?
topic: The page ends a number-theoretic argument, asks how the quadratic extension obtained from the roots of a cubic equation relates to the cubic base field, and sets out a plan to apply the ideal concept to all mathematical disciplines, as Lie did with the group concept.

triage.modern_statement: Let K be a non-Galois cubic number field and let L be its splitting field, the field generated by all roots of the cubic. L is a sextic field with Galois group S3. It is a quadratic extension of K and a cyclic cubic extension of the quadratic field k = Q(√d), where d is the discriminant of the cubic. Hilbert asks what happens when the relevant relative discriminant is 1, meaning the extension is unramified at every finite prime. Read in the most likely way, the question is: when is the cyclic cubic extension L/k unramified, and how do such cubic fields relate to the ideal-class group of k? In modern terms: unramified cyclic cubic extensions of a quadratic field k correspond to subgroups of index 3 in the class group of k. They exist exactly when 3 divides the class number of k, and they arise as splitting fields of cubic fields whose discriminant equals the fundamental discriminant d. The note's wording is slightly ambiguous: 'that cubic field' could mean the cubic relative field L over k, or the quadratic extension L/K. In either reading, the question belongs to the theory of unramified extensions, i.e., class field theory.
triage.answered_by: Class field theory in general: Hilbert's own class-field conjectures of the late 1890s, proved by Takagi around 1920. For the cubic case specifically: Helmut Hasse, 'Arithmetische Theorie der kubischen Zahlkörper auf klassenkörpertheoretischer Grundlage', Mathematische Zeitschrift 31 (1930), 565–582. Arnold Scholz continued this work, e.g. 'Idealklassen und Einheiten in kubischen Körpern' (1933). Later explicit work includes Honda's construction of cubic polynomials defining unramified cubic extensions of quadratic fields.

evidence.claim: Hasse's 1930 paper in Math. Z. 31, pp. 565–582, develops the arithmetic theory of cubic fields on a class-field-theoretic basis.
Scholz's 1933 paper on ideal classes and units in cubic fields builds on Hasse's 1930 class-field-theoretic treatment of cubic fields.
This is standard class field theory: a cyclic 3-class group gives a unique unramified cyclic cubic extension of the quadratic field, linked to a non-Galois cubic field with the matching discriminant.
Modern work still studies unramified cubic extensions of quadratic fields through the 3-part of the class group, including Honda's cubic polynomials that define these extensions.

triage.why: The note asks about the splitting field of a cubic as a quadratic extension of the cubic field and focuses on relative discriminant 1. That is the defining property of an unramified extension, which is the central object of the class field theory Hilbert himself began. The basic question was settled by class field theory, and for cubic fields explicitly by Hasse in 1930: such unramified cubic relative fields over Q(√d) correspond to 3-divisibility of the class number of Q(√d). This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems, although it is close in spirit to Problem 9 (the general reciprocity law) and Problem 12 (constructing class fields explicitly). Related questions are still actively studied, such as 3-class groups, unramified 3-extensions and class field towers. I could not see the diary page, and the note is short and ambiguous, so linking it to exactly this question is my interpretation. That is why confidence is medium rather than high.
